title: How To Manage Performance Pressure And Anxiety
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses acute teacher anxiety and pressure that lifestyle strategies like breathing exercises, sleep, and hobbies fail to fully resolve, offering a single in-the-moment technique: deliberate, frequent pausing. He describes how stressed teachers tend to talk fast, run sentences together, and speak with a nervous pitch, and argues this transmits their internal tension directly into the classroom, making students restless and increasingly prone to misbehavior in a self-reinforcing loop. His remedy is to consciously slow down through repeated pausing — before breaths, before movement, before topic changes, even mid-sentence — until it becomes exaggerated and slightly uncomfortable, gradually resetting both the teacher's physiological state and the classroom's overall rhythm. He frames the payoff as twofold: lower personal stress and better student behavior, concluding that freedom from performance pressure and perfectionism directly increases a teacher's effectiveness and happiness.
points: Standard stress-reduction strategies — breathing, exercise, sleep, hobbies — sometimes aren't enough when pressure is acute, requiring an in-the-moment technique.
Stressed teachers tend to talk fast with a nervous pitch, which transmits tension directly to students and increases restlessness and misbehavior.
The recommended technique is deliberate, repeated pausing — before breaths, movement, topic changes, even mid-sentence — until the classroom's pace visibly slows.
Slowing one's own pace through pausing resets the classroom's rhythm and reduces the self-reinforcing loop of teacher tension and student agitation.
Freedom from performance pressure and perfectionism is presented as directly increasing both a teacher's effectiveness and personal happiness.
quotes: The daily pressure of the job causes many teachers to experience anxiety.
You see, teachers who are stressed and feeling pressure to perform tend to talk fast and with a high, nervous pitch. They run their sentences together.
They fill their room with the same tension they feel on the inside, which causes students to become restless, excitable, and agitated.
Pause before taking a breath. Pause before moving. Pause before changing topics. Pause in the middle of a sentence. Pause after one word and then the next.
Do this through conscious pausing and you’ll start feeling a lot better. You’ll breathe easier, deeper, and slower.
That you’re so much more effective, and so much happier, when you’re free from the performance and perfectionism ties that bind you.
